title: A MRI-Based Toolbox for Neurosurgical Planning in Nonhuman Primates
protocol: Transport the monkey to a 3T MRI scanner.
Place the animal in an MR-compatible stereotaxic frame.
Record standard T1 anatomical MR images with specified parameters.
Load the T1 MPRAGE scan into MR imaging software.
Select "Extract Brain (BET)" from the Plugins dropdown menu.
Set the intensity threshold around 0.5−0.7 and the threshold gradient value to 0.
Repeatedly use the extraction function at successively lower intensity thresholds until the scan contains only the cortical anatomy.
Under the region of interest (ROI) menu, select Threshold to ROI and choose Shrink Wrap and 3D options.
Choose a threshold value around 600 to isolate the brain from surrounding tissue.
Select OK to form the bitmap.
To create a surface, select Build Surface under the image menu and input the threshold used in step 2.3.
Select OK to finalize the surface creation.
Save the extracted brain ROI as a .nii or .nii.gz file for future use.
Load the saved brain extraction data into medical image processing software.
From the modules toolbar, hover over welcome to slicer and move to all modules.
Select Editor functionality from the menu.
Click OK on the popup warning.
Select Threshold Effect from the Editor module menu.
Adjust threshold range sliders so the portion of the bitmap containing the brain is highlighted in all three slices.
Apply the adjusted settings.
Open the model maker module and select the bitmap file generated in step 3.3 from the input volumes dropdown menu.
Under Models, create a new model hierarchy.
Assign the name of the model to the hierarchy and select Apply to create the volume.
Save the file in the .stl format.
Load the extracted brain model into computer aided design software by opening the .prt file.
Under the features section of the insert menu, select Convert to Mesh body.
Select the Graphic body of the brain and convert it.
Click the Sketch button and select the top plane as the sketch plane.
Draw a rectangle containing either the entirety of the right or left hemisphere of the brain.
Select the extrude boss/base feature while in the sketch.
Extrude a cubic rectangle to contain the top part of the brain.
Convert to Mesh body under the features section of the ‘insert’ menu.
Select the extruded cube in the Solid bodies folder and convert it.
To create the negative space, subtract the model of the brain from the newly extruded cube using the Combine feature and selecting the subtract option.
Repeat steps for the other hemisphere of the brain (left or right).
Save the resulting files as a .stl for 3D printing and a .prt for further manipulation.
Create a sketch in the top plane and draw a rectangle containing either the entirety of the right or left hemisphere of the brain.
Select the extrude boss/base feature while in the sketch and extrude with the Offset from Plane feature selected.
Offset the extrusion up to a distance where there are no overhanging contours in the brain anatomy, capturing just the upper anatomy.
Under the features section of the ‘insert’ menu, select Convert to Mesh body.
Select the extruded cube in the Solid bodies folder and convert it.
To create the negative space, subtract the model of the brain from the newly extruded cube using the Combine feature and selecting the subtract option.
Create a sketch plane on the dorsal side of the mold.
Select Convert Entities and then select the sketch from step 4.3.1.

Select the extrude boss/base feature while in the sketch and, with the blind extrude option selected, extrude the solid body approximately 5 mm to completely enclose the subtracted brain anatomy in the mold.
Repeat steps 4.3.1−4.3.4 for the other hemisphere of the brain (left or right).
Save the resulting files as a .stl for 3D printing and a .prt for further manipulation.
By changing the dimensions and location of the cube and following the same protocol (steps 4.1 and 4.2), create molds that contain different parts of the brain.
Use ~70% infill density for 3D printing.
Increase the thickness of the outer shell to minimize leakage of the molding material.
Fill any gaps or defects in the print using nail polish or another binding agent.
Import the QUICK MPRAGE MRI from step 1.2 into matrix manipulation software as a DICOM file.
Combine all frames of the DICOM file into a 3D matrix if they are separate 2D frames.
Ensure each frame displays a coronal slice.
Create a binary mask by thresholding the 3D matrix using a greater than operator for individual pixel values.
Adjust the threshold to capture skull anatomy in the mask.
Process each frame from the 3D mask separately by grabbing a 2D slice from the mask.
Select 0 pixels from the corners of the frame in the “outside” layer as the “seed”.
Search neighboring 0’s until you encounter a 1 pixel, then continue searching until no more 0’s can be found.
Convert all connected 0’s to 1’s using the Matlab function “imfill” with inputs [MASK2] = imfill(MASK1,LOCATIONS,CONNECTIVITY).
Perform step 5.3 in all three dimensions of the data and keep them separate to mitigate information loss during skull removal.
Invert the values of the mask using the ~ operator (i.e., MASK2 = ~MASK1) to ensure “skull” is represented as 1’s while “outside” and “brain” are 0’s.

Create an index of all objects in each mask using the Matlab function “bwconncomp”, with the inputs and outputs being [CC] = bwconncomp(MASK), where MASK is the 3D mask matrix, and CC is a structural object containing the index values for each object.
Remove all objects except for the largest one from each mask by setting the values of smaller objects to 0’s.
Add the masks created from each pass together.
Compare the step size between each frame of the MRI to the dimensions of each pixel from the DICOM header.
Define a scale factor if the step size and pixel dimension differ, compensating for resolution differences between step size and pixel size for each voxel.
Add additional empty voxels to the 3D mask until the lowest resolution dimension is larger by a factor defined by the scale factor.
Linearly interpolate values in the mask until the mask fills the new space.
Export skull as an .stl file or similar filetype for 3D printing.
Manually identify the approximate location of the craniotomy from anatomical landmarks in the macaque brain atlas.
View an individual slice of the 3D matrix.
Scan forward or backward through the 3D matrix until recognizable anatomical landmarks are located.
Save the frame number as the z coordinate.
Use a data selection tool to save the x and y coordinates of a single point on this frame for the craniotomy centerpoint using the Matlab function “getpts”.
Convert the radius of the intended craniotomy from millimeters to voxels using the information in the DICOM header.

Set all voxels within the radius defined in step 6.2 to zero in the mask from step 5.8.4 using Supplemental coding file Craniotomy, where cranitomyMask is a 3D matrix with the craniotomy removed, and inputs are the initial 3D matrix, x, y, z coordinates of the centerpoint, radius, grid vectors of the 3D matrix, and resolution.
Export skull as an .stl file or similar filetype for 3D printing.
Repeat steps for each unique craniotomy.

Use a standard PLA printer and create G-Code with specified settings: inner density >50%, fast honeycomb internal fill pattern, rectilinear external fill pattern, plate temperature = 50 °C, extruder temperature = 230 °C.
Print prototypes and molds using specified settings.
Create G-Code for higher fidelity models of the brain and skull using an industrial-grade printer with ABS for the model and dissolvable support material.
Use Sparse - High Density fill style for printing high-fidelity models.
Dissolve the model in support solvent for ~12 h.
Press Start and watch the first layer of the print to ensure that the base layer is clean and even.
Patch any visible holes on the 3D printed molds with nail polish.
Combine agar powder and locust bean gum powder in a 1:4 ratio by mass.
Mix the powder mixture with phosphate buffered saline to achieve a 0.6% concentration solution.
Place the flask containing the solution in the microwave at maximum power for 2 minutes.
Stop the microwave when the solution begins to bubble, remove the flask, and swirl vigorously.
Return the flask to the microwave and continue heating until the full two minutes are complete.
Maintain swirling of the heated solution after removal from the microwave to prevent setting.
Run cold water on the outside of the flask to cool the solution while swirling.
Swirl the flask while transporting the solution to the mold to avoid premature hardening.
Pour the agarose solution into one of the brain molds until full.
Continue to swirl remaining solution in the flask.
Monitor the level of solution in the mold for leaks.
Refill the mold as necessary since the setting agarose will seal any leaks in the mold.
Allow the solution in the mold to sit unperturbed at room temperature until the solution has set and hardened into a solid.
Use a spatula to gently remove the gel model from the mold.
Place the gel model in a sealed container in a refrigerator.
Prepare the pump for infusion.
Fix the pump in a stereotaxic arm on a stereotaxic frame.
Position the pump to the correct injection trajectory and location normal to the surface of the gel model.
Fill a 250 µL syringe with DI water.
Mount the syringe onto the pump.
Withdraw DI water into the syringe completely through the cannula to fill it.
Use the pump driver to withdraw food coloring into the syringe to the target volume for injection.
Inject the food coloring slowly until a small bead forms at the tip of the cannula.
Dry the bead off the tip of the cannula.
Position the gel model under the cannula.
Lower the cannula until the tip touches the surface of the gel model.
Note the measurements on the stereotaxic arm.
Lower the cannula into the gel model quickly and smoothly to the target injection depth.
Ensure that the surface of the gel has sealed around the cannula.
Run the pump at a flowrate of 1 µL/min.
Increase the flowrate by 1 µL/min every minute until reaching 5 µL/min.
Observe the spread of the food coloring in the gel.
Remove the cannula from the gel quickly and smoothly.
Capture images of the spread of the food coloring.
Measure the dimensions of the embolism.
Calculate the ellipsoid volume of the injection.
